subject: physics
title: Acceleration and velocity–time graphs
key_idea: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes: the change in velocity divided by the time taken. On a velocity–time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area under the line is the distance travelled.

blocks.text: This section covers how to calculate acceleration from a change in velocity.

items.meaning: How quickly the velocity of an object changes.
An object that slows down is decelerating.
An acceleration that stays the same.

blocks.label: Acceleration
where: a is acceleration in metres per second squared (m/s²).
Δv is the change in velocity in metres per second (m/s).
v is the final velocity and u is the initial velocity, both in m/s.
t is the time taken in seconds (s).

items: Use the change in velocity, not the final velocity alone.
An object that slows down has a negative acceleration. This is called deceleration.

items.text: A train goes from 16 m/s to 25 m/s: Δv = 25 − 16 = 9 m/s.

diagram.alt: Calculate acceleration from the initial velocity, the final velocity and the time.
diagram.question: A train accelerates from {u} m/s to {v} m/s in {t} s. Calculate the acceleration.

items: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken, in m/s².
Always use the change in velocity.
A negative acceleration means the object is decelerating.

blocks.text: This section covers the equation for uniform acceleration that links velocity, acceleration and distance.

blocks.label: Uniform acceleration
where: v is the final velocity in metres per second (m/s).
u is the initial velocity in metres per second (m/s).
a is the acceleration in metres per second squared (m/s²).
s is the distance in metres (m), sometimes written x.

items: If the object starts from rest, u = 0.
If the object comes to rest, v = 0.
Finding v or u: take the square root at the end.
Convert distances to metres first, for example 0.018 km = 18 m.

items.text: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 5.0 m/s² over 45 m: v² − 0² = 2 × 5.0 × 45
v² = 450, so v = 21 m/s to 2 significant figures.

diagram.alt: Change the initial velocity, acceleration and distance to see the final velocity.

items: The equation linking v, u, a and s applies to uniform acceleration only.
Starting from rest means u = 0. Coming to rest means v = 0.
Take the square root to find a velocity.

blocks.text: This section covers what the gradient and the area of a velocity–time graph tell you.

rows: Constant velocity. The acceleration is zero.

items: The acceleration is the gradient of the velocity–time graph.
To find the acceleration, divide the change in velocity by the change in time between two points on the line.
The distance travelled is the area between the graph line and the time axis.
For a straight line, split the area into a rectangle and a triangle, or count squares.
Comparing two lines: the steeper line has the greater acceleration.
Gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration.
Area under a velocity–time graph is distance travelled.
A horizontal line means constant velocity.

checks.q: The velocity of a pin changes from 0 to 12 m/s in 0.15 s. Calculate the acceleration.
A lorry travels 84 m with a constant acceleration of 2.0 m/s² and reaches 19 m/s. Calculate its initial velocity.
State what the gradient and the area under a velocity–time graph represent.
checks.a: The gradient is the acceleration. The area is the distance travelled.

worked_example.question: A car accelerates at 5.0 m/s² over a distance of 45 m. The initial velocity of the car is 0 m/s. Calculate the final velocity of the car. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
worked_example.tip: One mark each for substituting, finding v², taking the square root and rounding to 2 significant figures.

items: (AQA: Higher tier) The distance travelled, or the displacement, is the area under a velocity–time graph. Measure the area by counting squares when needed.
Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s².

worked_example.question: A car travelling at 15 m/s comes to rest in a distance of 14 m when the brakes are applied. Calculate the deceleration of the car. Use an equation selected from the list of equations.
worked_example.tip: Choose the equation that links velocities, acceleration and distance. Rearrangement and substitution can be in either order. 225 ÷ 28 scores 2 marks. A negative sign is accepted.

blocks.text: Calculating acceleration from the gradient and distance from the area is for uniform acceleration only.

worked_example.question: Car B brakes and comes to a stop. The deceleration of car B is 6 m/s². The initial speed of the car is 18 m/s. Calculate the braking distance of car B.
worked_example.tip: A correct answer of 27 m scores all 3 marks. A correct substitution into the unrearranged equation earns 1 mark.
